name: Eating for jaw (chewing hard foods)

card.summary: Chewing tough foods to grow the masseter; the muscle can enlarge with heavy chewing, but hard-food diets are untested.
card.note: Overuse of the jaw is associated with TMJ problems in reference material.

quick.overview:
Eating for jaw means chewing hard, chewy foods to build the masseter and define the jawline.

The masseter can enlarge with habitual clenching or gum chewing, but no studies test hard-food diets for looks.
quick.mechanism: Repeated loading of the jaw-closing muscles may enlarge them, as seen with bruxism and constant gum chewing.
quick.risks: Reference material links masseter enlargement to facial asymmetry and temporomandibular joint problems.

chain: Repeated chewing of tough foods loads the masseter
Muscle at the jaw angle may thicken
angle.text: People chew tough foods hoping to thicken the masseter, since this muscle's enlargement is known to widen the lower face in people who clench or chew gum heavily. The jawline effect is the claimed outcome of food chewing specifically.

lead: Eating for jaw is the practice of regularly chewing tough or hard foods, such as raw carrots, tough meats or dense chewy items, with the aim of building the masseter and giving the lower face a stronger, more defined jawline. Practitioners in looksmaxxing communities discuss it alongside mastic gum and jaw exercisers as a food-based way to train the chewing muscles.[2][12]

The idea rests on the masseter, the main jaw-closing muscle, which is one of the strongest chewing muscles.[1] Reference material reports that it can enlarge in people who habitually clench or grind their teeth or chew gum constantly, typically painlessly and sometimes unevenly between sides, and that this enlargement can change the contour of the lower face.[1][7] Proponents extend that logic to hard foods: more chewing load, a fuller muscle at the angle of the jaw.

Forum users also discuss hard chewing for effects on bone, including jaw width and maxilla development, and some cite animal research on soft diets and craniofacial growth.[2] No human trial has tested a hard-food diet for facial appearance. Studies of chewing loads concern the temporomandibular joint and dental function rather than looks.[3][4]

paras: The masseter elevates the jaw and is among the strongest chewing muscles; it has superficial, deep and coronoid heads, and its superficial fibers can also push the jaw forward.[1] It is one of four muscles of mastication and is the most superficial of them, lying over the angle of the lower jaw where the lower face's width is set.[1]

Reference material reports that habitual clenching, bruxism and constant gum chewing can enlarge it, usually without symptoms, and that uneven enlargement can cause facial asymmetry.[1] Enlargement of the jaw-moving muscles, especially the masseter, is listed as a sign of bruxism and a typical finding in its diagnosis.[7] The same source notes an association with temporomandibular joint problems, and that people sometimes seek care because of comments on their facial appearance.[1]

On looksmax.org, users ask whether chewing hard foods such as carrots can widen the jaw or maxilla. In one thread a 17-year-old asks whether biting large amounts of carrot daily could widen the maxilla and whether similar hard foods exist. One reply advises chewing with the molars rather than the front teeth, since front teeth are not built for heavy chewing, suggests that ramus growth and jaw widening are possible while maxillary widening is less likely, and posts an animal study on hypofunctional jaw muscles and craniofacial growth.[2] In another thread a user states that hard foods will not make the jaw bigger, and a reply points to the maxilla and nose as the features that stand out in the poster's photos, mentioning jaw surgery and rhinoplasty as alternatives.[5]

Hard chewing is discussed with other food-and-chewing routines: mastic gum, a resin traditionally chewed for centuries and produced mainly on the Greek island of Chios, is a common companion, as are jaw exercisers.[11] Wikipedia notes that chewing gum has a long history, including an 1869 US patent for a gum meant to clean teeth and strengthen the jaw.[10]

The practice also sits beside mewing, the tongue-posture technique named after British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike, which spread through social media from about 2019 and is especially popular in looksmaxxing subcultures.[8] John Mew's orthotropics also involved dietary changes alongside palatal expansion and tongue posture, according to Wikipedia, though the article does not detail the diet.[9] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article places mewing under softmaxxing and jaw surgery under hardmaxxing, and reports that doctors have criticised mewing as misinformation.[12]

A 2025 study in Journal of Biological Engineering examined how chewing loads alter temporomandibular joint metabolism in rats fed hard or soft food, including a group switched from soft to hard food; it looked at joint bone and cartilage rather than facial shape.[3] A 2025 PLoS One study of 120 patients with temporomandibular disorders found that chewing hard foods was the most affected jaw activity in the arthralgia group.[4] These look at joint health, not facial shape.

Enlargement of the masseter in people who clench, grind or chew gum constantly is described in reference material, and the muscle responds to heavy load like other skeletal muscle.[1][7] Whether a diet of tough foods supplies enough load, and whether any enlargement would be visible, has not been studied. Botulinum toxin injection into the masseter is used for bruxism, and an overview of systematic reviews reported reduced pain and sleep bruxism frequency, with disuse of the muscle reducing later dosing needs; it is a related route for contouring the same muscle in the opposite direction.[7]

On bone, reviewers of orthotropics report that the evidence for its effectiveness is inadequate, and the American Association of Orthodontists is reported to say there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw.[8][9] A 2024 study of orthognathic surgery patients reported that they still had difficulty chewing hard foods three months after surgery, showing how closely jaw function and diet are linked in clinical practice.[13]

Dental literature describes cracked tooth syndrome, an incomplete fracture of a back tooth, as a recognized condition with varied symptoms, which relates to the force that very hard foods place on teeth.[6] Reference material links masseter enlargement to facial asymmetry when uneven and to temporomandibular joint pathology,[1] though the link between bruxism and temporomandibular dysfunction is debated, with a systematic review reporting a positive link with TMD pain when bruxism was self-reported and a much weaker one with stricter diagnostic criteria.[7]

Regarding mastic gum, the European Medicines Agency in 2016 found clinical studies on mastic too small to show well-established use, and advised against its use in children and during pregnancy and breastfeeding.[11]

No studies found on hard-food diets and facial appearance. Related research concerns chewing loads on the temporomandibular joint,[3] jaw function in temporomandibular disorders,[4] botulinum toxin treatment for bruxism,[7] a study of post-meal chewing gum and occlusion after orthodontic treatment,[10] and tooth fracture.[6]

timeline.event: US patent granted to dentist William F. Semple for a chewing gum intended to clean teeth and strengthen the jaw.[10]
John Mew proposes the 'Tropic Premise', which he later develops into orthotropics, according to Wikipedia.[9]
Review of cracked tooth syndrome in the Journal of the Canadian Dental Association.[6]
EMA assessment of mastic as a traditional herbal medicine.[11]
Mewing draws mainstream media coverage and spreads across social media.[8][9]
Mike Mew is struck from the UK dental register, according to Wikipedia.[8]
Studies on chewing loads in the temporomandibular joint and jaw limitation in TMD.[3][4]

lore.intro: Hard-food chewing is discussed on looksmax.org as a jaw and maxilla training habit, with members split on whether it does anything for adults.[2][5]

claims.claim: Chewing hard foods like carrots can widen the jaw or maxilla.
claims.believers: A poster asks about biting carrots daily, and a reply suggests ramus growth and jaw widening are plausible, citing an animal study on soft diets and jaw muscles.[2]
claims.experts: Reference material describes masseter enlargement from habitual clenching and gum chewing; no human studies have tested hard-food diets for jaw width or appearance.[1]

claims.claim: Hard foods will not change an adult jaw.
claims.believers: Another looksmax.org user states hard foods will not enlarge the jaw.[5]
claims.experts: No published human trial has tested the question either way.

claims.claim: Chew with the molars, not the front teeth.
claims.believers: A reply advises using the molars because front teeth are not meant for heavy chewing.[2]
claims.experts: Dental literature describes cracked tooth syndrome as a recognized condition of back teeth under high force.[6]

claims.claim: A strong chewing muscle gives a wider, more defined lower face.
claims.believers: Proponents reason from people whose masseters enlarge with habitual gum chewing or clenching.[1][2]
claims.experts: Reference material confirms masseter enlargement can alter the lower-face contour and may cause asymmetry if uneven.[1]

claims.claim: Hard chewing can strain the jaw joint.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org user states that hard foods will not make the jaw bigger, and posters discuss alternatives such as surgery.[5]
claims.experts: A 2025 study of 120 TMD patients found chewing hard foods was the most affected activity in the arthralgia group, and reference material links masseter enlargement with TMJ problems.[1][4]
